title: Mazhabi Sikhs
hook: Sikhs from Dalit backgrounds, heirs of Bhai Jaita, who served in honored regiments

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sikhs of Assam, who carried the Guru into new ground. Your line was stayed far away. What did your faraway someone say they still keep from home? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-one.

A man walks out of Delhi at night with a bundle held close against his chest. He keeps off the main roads. Every checkpoint is a danger; every stranger might ask what he's carrying. What he carries is the head of Guru Tegh Bahadur, executed in the city. He is taking it to the Guru's young son, far to the north. Two days ago we followed the trader who carried the Guru's body home; this is the other road out of Delhi. His name, in Sikh memory, is Bhai Jaita. He came from a family that the society around him counted among the lowest. Today we meet the Sikhs who call him their own.
screen: `A BUNDLE CARRIED OUT OF DELHI.` → `THE HEAD OF GURU TEGH BAHADUR.` → `BHAI JAITA, COUNTED AMONG THE LOWEST.`

segments.voice: Mazhabi Sikhs are Sikhs from Dalit backgrounds, from communities the caste order pushed to its bottom rung. In the panth they honor Bhai Jaita as their forebear. Here is the rest of the story as tradition tells it. Bhai Jaita reached Anandpur and laid the Guru's head before the young Guru Gobind Singh. The Guru embraced him and spoke a phrase Sikhs still repeat: the Rangretas are the Guru's own sons. Rangreta is a name tradition uses for Bhai Jaita's people. In a single sentence, a community the world treated as outcast was claimed as family by the Guru himself. Tradition remembers Bhai Jaita later taking amrit and fighting beside the Guru. Mazhabi Sikhs carried that courage into later centuries. They served in regiments of the army that are known for their battle honors, and those regiments are a point of deep pride. The story has a harder side too. The Gurus' teaching on caste is plain, but caste prejudice has not vanished among Sikhs any more than among others. In places, Mazhabi Sikhs have faced exclusion, even in matters of worship. Sikh voices have long spoken against that, citing the Gurus. Here is one of those lines. Guru Nanak, in Raag Asa on Ang 349, says in paraphrase: recognize the light in each person, and don't ask about caste; in what lies ahead, there is no caste. The Guru's embrace at Anandpur was that line lived out. The man carrying the Guru's head through the dark was family. The phrase the Guru's own sons isn't a compliment. It's a claim the panth is still asked to live up to.
screen: `MAZHABI SIKHS: FROM DALIT BACKGROUNDS.` · `ANANDPUR: THE GURU'S EMBRACE.` · `HONORED REGIMENTS, AND HARD PREJUDICE.` · `ANG 349: SEE THE LIGHT, NOT THE CASTE.` · then, large: `THE GURU'S OWN SONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor someone overlooked. Settle into a few slow breaths. Then let someone come to mind whose work or worth goes unseen: a person who works the night shift, who mends what others break, who's never invited to the front. Recall one thing they've done that mattered. Breathe in, and see the light in them, plainly, without a label. Breathe out, and hold their name as you would a family member's. If you pray, you can rest on Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Mazhabi Sikhs. Sikhs from Dalit backgrounds who honor Bhai Jaita as their forebear, and whom tradition says the Guru called his own sons. Today's word.
Your line: the guru's own sons. Today, learn the name of one person you see often but have never really noticed, and use it when you thank them. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-one.
